title: Do Common Core Professional Development Like This
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Responding to a survey in which nearly half of teachers rated their Common Core training as less than high quality, Stuart lays out how to run standards PD that empowers rather than burdens a staff. He begins with ultimate goals, framing the Core around college and career readiness rather than test scores or minutiae lists. He argues that PD leaders must know the standards deeply but should not force every teacher to wade through them, since handing out full standards lists produces either frantic coverage, resentment or paralysis. Instead, leaders should offer a simple-but-deep framework, concrete next steps such as pop-up debate, and open conversation about what teachers already do well, so that both novices and experts stay engaged. He also defends including character in the framework because noncognitive strengths are what get students to actually do the harder reading, writing and arguing the standards require.
points: Stuart opens PD by asking teachers to state their ultimate aim for students in one sentence and then showing how college and career readiness aligns with it.
Handing every teacher a printout of all grade-level standards, he argues, produces a crapshoot of frantic coverage, angry dismissal or paralysis.
The facilitator, not the whole staff, should master the standards documents and boil them into a framework simple enough to grasp in an hour yet deep enough to explore for years.
Overcomplicated PD leaves participants frustrated or planning tomorrow's lesson, whereas a simplified framework engages both low- and high-skill teachers as professionals.
Character belongs in standards PD because noncognitive strengths are what make students willing to take on complex reading, writing and argument.
quotes: I then show how the Common Core is aimed at something similar — not at test scores or stressing teachers out with minutiae lists or whatever. The standards aim at college and career readiness — and that's something we ought to want for all of our students.

In other words, if you tell your teachers, “Teach the Common Core” and then give them a printout of every grade-level standard applicable to them, you are going to get a crazy crapshoot of results. Some teachers will go about revamping their whole curricula, insanely trying to “get to” or “cover” each one of the standards.

And just for the record, that latter teacher isn't necessarily ineffective. When we start saying “Effective teachers are those who adhere to standards — 'nuff said,” we start to create a toxic environment for high-performing teachers.
The goal should be a way of organizing the standards so that they are simple enough to understand in an hour or so, yet deep enough to explore for years.

When we overcomplicate things in PD, the majority of participants are sitting there frustrated, stressed out, annoyed, or planning tomorrow's lesson on a piece of scratch paper, and we're spending a ton of time explaining the overcomplicated concepts.

But when you bring a simplified framework that participants can grasp in an hour, people tend to be engaged at both the low-skill and high-skill ends of your faculty spectrum. It engages their professionalism because they say, “Yes, I can do this,” and also, “There's room to develop this into something really cool.

Some well-meaning educators say, “Well, the majority of students today will only read if we let them pick what they read or confer with them extensively or [insert something else].” But I don't think that's true. I think kids are unlikely to engage with a challenge if we don't teach them to do so, but I think they are likely to do it if we teach them how.
